speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

How long does each episode of vertigo typically last? Do they last less than a minute, between 1 and 10 minutes, or longer than 20 minutes? Also, does the spinning sensation occur only when you change your head position (like rolling over in bed or looking up)?

The patient script continues to deny headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, or recent infections, which makes vestibular migraine and Meniere's disease less likely given the lack of auditory or vestibular migraine symptoms. Since the script remains static regarding duration and positional triggers despite my specific questions, I must rely on the physical exam results to differentiate between Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) and other causes. Can you confirm if the vertigo is strictly triggered by specific head movements, such as rolling over in bed or looking up?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Manoeuvre: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV; Head Impulse Test: Not specified in available data.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) of the posterior canal. The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver with right-sided horizontal nystagmus confirms the diagnosis, especially given the absence of auditory symptoms and prior infection history.
